keyIdea.title: Navigation focus
keyIdea.text: Explicit focus and navigation rules turn an accessible UI into a dependable one for keyboard and gamepad players.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Navigation & Patterns
Focus Controls
SetUserFocus
Force a widget to receive gamepad/keyboard navigation from a player controller. Use when a menu opens so the first actionable item is selected.
SetKeyboardFocus
Set explicit keyboard focus for text entry or for the primary button. Avoid leaving focus undefined to prevent controller users from being stuck.
Navigation Rules
Override automatic navigation in UMG to guarantee predictable Up/Down/Left/Right moves between buttons.
Common UI Patterns
Pause Menu — UIOnly, pause game, show cursor, focus first button.
Inventory — UIOnly or GameAndUI depending on design. If you drag items, prefer UIOnly.
Pop-up Dialog — Overlay that may temporarily grab UIOnly, return focus when dismissed.

screens.title: Input Modes — GameOnly, UIOnly, GameAndUI
screens.narratorSegment: Input modes control whether input is handled by gameplay code, by widgets, or by both. GameOnly directs everything to the game, which is the default: movement, shooting, and camera controls remain active and UI widgets do not receive keyboard or gamepad input unless they explicitly request it. UIOnly sends all relevant input to the UI layer and disables gameplay input; this is ideal for full-screen menus and inventories where clicking, dragging, and keyboard navigation must be reliable. GameAndUI is a hybrid: it forwards input to both systems and can be useful for RTS-style interactions or context cursors. The important practical point is that GameAndUI often creates conflicts: a mouse click intended to press a UI button may also trigger a game action unless you consume the event. A common pattern is to switch to UIOnly and show the cursor when opening a menu, then restore GameOnly and hide the cursor when closing. Concrete example: when opening a pause menu you typically call SetInputMode(FInputModeUIOnly()) and set bShowMouseCursor to true; on resume, SetInputMode(FInputModeGameOnly()) and hide the cursor. Misconception to avoid: using GameAndUI to “be safe” usually leads to duplicate actions; prefer explicit consumption of input or UIOnly for modal dialogs. Takeaway: choose the strictest mode that matches your interaction model and manage cursor visibility and focus together.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Input Modes
Definition
Input Mode selects the destination of input events: game, UI, or both.
  • GameOnly — default; widgets don't receive keyboard/gamepad.
  • UIOnly — all input goes to UI; game input disabled; cursor shown.
  • GameAndUI — both receive input; manage consumption carefully.
Concrete Example
Opening a pause menu: pause the game, AddToViewport the widget, SetInputMode(UIOnly) with the widget focused, and set bShowMouseCursor = true.
Common Mistake
Using GameAndUI without consuming input leads to clicks triggering UI and gameplay. Prefer UIOnly for modal interactions.
Key Takeaway

Select the strictest input mode that matches user expectations and manage cursor visibility and focus to avoid surprises.

Process: Toggling Input Mode (visualized)
Open Menu → Pause game → Add widget → SetInputMode(UIOnly) → Show cursor → Set focus
Close Menu → Remove/hide widget → SetInputMode(GameOnly) → Hide cursor → Restore gameplay focus
Quick check: if clicking a UI element also fires a weapon, you likely left input in a mixed state. Revisit your SetInputMode and event consumption.

screens.title: Implementing TogglePauseMenu in AMyPlayerController
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the TogglePauseMenu implementation and the runtime consequences of each call. The pattern begins by checking a boolean bIsGamePaused. If paused, we resume gameplay: SetGamePaused(false), clear the pause widget from the viewport or hide it if you'll reuse it, set input back to GameOnly, and hide the mouse cursor. If not paused, we pause the game, create the pause widget via CreateWidget with a stored PauseMenuWidgetClass, AddToViewport, and then set the input mode to UIOnly. When using UIOnly you should call InputMode. SetWidgetToFocus with the widget's TakeWidget result so the engine knows where to send navigation events. Also set the mouse lock behavior as needed and set bShowMouseCursor to true. A concrete runtime example: press the Pause key, the game pauses, the menu fades in, the first button receives focus, and controller sticks move between buttons predictably. A common misconception is to RemoveFromParent() on every close; if you expect frequent toggles, prefer SetVisibility(Collapsed) so the widget remains in memory and costs less on reopen. Finally, ensure your resume path clears animation timers and any temporary input bindings to prevent stale state after unpausing. Try to test both keyboard and gamepad paths.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › TogglePauseMenu Walkthrough
Code Example
// In AMyPlayerController.cpp - simplified and escaped for display
void AMyPlayerController::TogglePauseMenu()
{
    if (bIsGamePaused)
    {
        UGameplayStatics::SetGamePaused(GetWorld(), false);
        bIsGamePaused = false;

        if (PauseMenuWidget)
        {
            PauseMenuWidget->RemoveFromParent();
            PauseMenuWidget = nullptr;
        }

        FInputModeGameOnly InputMode;
        SetInputMode(InputMode);
        bShowMouseCursor = false;
    }
    else
    {
        UGameplayStatics::SetGamePaused(GetWorld(), true);
        bIsGamePaused = true;

        if (PauseMenuWidgetClass)
        {
            PauseMenuWidget = CreateWidget<UUserWidget>(this, PauseMenuWidgetClass);
            if (PauseMenuWidget)
            {
                PauseMenuWidget->AddToViewport();
            }
        }

        FInputModeUIOnly InputMode;
        InputMode.SetWidgetToFocus(PauseMenuWidget->TakeWidget());
        InputMode.SetLockMouseToViewportBehavior(EMouseLockMode::DoNotLock);
        SetInputMode(InputMode);
        bShowMouseCursor = true;
    }
}
Explanation & Runtime Steps
  1. Pause flag flips and UGameplayStatics::SetGamePaused controls Tick and time dilation for many systems.
  2. Widget creation and AddToViewport present UI; consider reusing widgets to avoid allocation costs.
  3. SetInputMode with SetWidgetToFocus routes navigation; forgetting focus can break gamepad use.
  4. bShowMouseCursor toggles the OS cursor; remember to hide it when returning to gameplay.
Pro tip

If reopen speed matters, hide (Collapsed) instead of RemoveFromParent to avoid recreation overhead.

screens.title: Widget Animation Binding and PlayAnimation
screens.narratorSegment: Widget animations provide important visual feedback and polish for menus and overlays. In UMG you author animations in the Designer and then bind them to C++ by adding a UPROPERTY marked Transient and meta=(BindWidgetAnim) of type UWidgetAnimation*. When the widget class is used as the blueprint parent, Unreal will populate that pointer if the animation name matches. In NativeConstruct you can detect the bound animation and call PlayAnimation to start it. A concrete example: create a FadeIn animation that adjusts Render Opacity from 0 to 1 over 0.5 seconds for your pause Canvas Panel. In the generated UMyPauseMenuWidget C++ subclass you add UPROPERTY(Transient, meta=(BindWidgetAnim)) UWidgetAnimation* FadeInAnimation; and in NativeConstruct call PlayAnimation(FadeInAnimation). A common misconception is that BindWidgetAnim magically creates animations; it only binds existing blueprint animations to the C++ pointer. Another pitfall is playing animations on a widget that hasn't been added to the viewport yet—ensure AddToViewport happens before relying on visible results, or play the animation inside NativeConstruct of the widget itself if it is constructed before AddToViewport. Takeaway: bind animations for predictable code-driven polish and always verify the animation pointer before calling PlayAnimation.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Widget Animation
C++ Binding Pattern
// In MyPauseMenuWidget.h
UPROPERTY(Transient, meta=(BindWidgetAnim))
UWidgetAnimation* FadeInAnimation;

// In MyPauseMenuWidget.cpp
void UMyPauseMenuWidget::NativeConstruct()
{
    Super::NativeConstruct();
    if (FadeInAnimation)
    {
        PlayAnimation(FadeInAnimation);
    }
}
Practical Notes
  • BindWidgetAnim requires the animation name to match the blueprint animation.
  • Play animations in NativeConstruct for consistent playback when constructed.
  • Ensure widget is visible to the player when playing animations or you may not see the effect.
Key Takeaway

Bind blueprint animations to C++ pointers and play them in NativeConstruct for reliable, code-driven polish.

screens.title: Visibility: RemoveFromParent vs Hidden vs Collapsed
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing how to hide UI affects performance, memory, and state retention. RemoveFromParent completely removes the widget from the viewport and breaks its link to the widget tree: the object is typically eligible for garbage collection unless you keep a reference. This is good when you only show a widget once and want to free memory. Hidden keeps the widget in the hierarchy and reserves layout space, but it is not rendered; Collapsed keeps the widget in memory and removes it from layout so it consumes less render cost and no layout space. For frequently toggled UIs like a pause menu that opens many times per session, prefer Collapsed or Hidden because AddToViewport and construction are relatively expensive. A concrete example: if you RemoveFromParent every time and the player toggles the menu repeatedly, you will allocate and deallocate the widget repeatedly which can cause frame hitches. A common misconception is that Hidden equals zero cost; Hidden still keeps layout data and bindings active. Collapsed is often the best balance when you want the widget available but not visible. Takeaway: match the lifecycle to usage frequency—remove rarely used or large, persistent widgets and collapse frequently toggled ones to keep responsiveness.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Visibility & Performance
Behaviour Comparison
RemoveFromParent()
Unregisters and frees the widget. Use for rare, large UI elements you don't need again soon.
Hidden
Keeps layout space and bindings; not rendered. Use when layout must remain stable.
Collapsed
Keeps widget in memory but removes it from layout and render—best for frequent toggles.
Concrete Scenario
If your pause menu opens dozens of times in a session, creating it once and using Collapsed to hide it avoids repeated allocations and reduces frame spikes. If you have a large, one-off settings screen only accessible in the main menu, RemoveFromParent may be preferable.
Key Takeaway

Favor Collapsed for responsiveness, Hidden when layout must stay, and RemoveFromParent when you need to free memory.

screens.title: Designing Reusable UI with Child Widgets
screens.narratorSegment: Complex screens should be composed from smaller child widgets to improve maintainability and performance. Instead of a monolithic pause menu blueprint with dozens of elements and logic, split the UI into a header widget, a menu actions widget, and an optional settings pane. Each child can manage its own bindings, animation, and input handling. This modular approach reduces per-frame cost because only active child widgets update when necessary and you can reuse the same child across different parent screens. A concrete example: a reusable ButtonRow widget used in the pause menu and in the inventory context menus. When you change the visual style or behavior, you update it in one place and all parents benefit. Also, smaller widgets make navigation rules easier: set explicit navigation for each child so moving between rows is predictable. A common misconception is that more widgets always cost more—actually, smaller, reusable widgets can be cheaper than a large single widget because they localize bindings and reduce conditional logic. Takeaway: design with reuse in mind; child widgets are a both a code organization and a performance tool.

keyIdea.title: Modular UI

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › Reusable UI Architecture
Architecture Sketch
HeaderWidget — title, back button, small state display
MenuActionsWidget — button list, handles focus rules for its items
SettingsPaneWidget — optional child loaded on demand, can be Collapsed
Each child widget manages its own events and animations. The parent concerns itself with high-level input mode and focus routing.
Benefits
  • Reusability across menus and screens.
  • Simpler navigation: each child defines clear entry and exit focus points.
  • Performance: smaller widgets can reduce per-frame overhead when used with visibility states.
Key Takeaway

Organize UI as composable widgets to reduce complexity and improve runtime behavior.

screens.title: UI Navigation Rules and Predictable Gamepad Flow
screens.narratorSegment: Predictable navigation is essential for players using a gamepad or keyboard. By default, UMG attempts automatic navigation, but complex layouts can introduce jumps or skipped widgets. To achieve consistent behavior you should set explicit navigation rules for each focusable widget in the Designer or at runtime via SetNavigationRule. When a menu opens, call SetUserFocus on the first actionable widget so sticks and D-pad presses move from a known start. A concrete example: in a Vertical Box of three buttons, explicitly set Down for the first button to the second, and Up for the second to the first. This avoids layout-based surprises when nested panels or anchors change the implicit order. Misconception: relying solely on tab order or placement is brittle; changing visual layout can break navigation. Another tool is Widget->SetKeyboardFocus for text fields to ensure typing input goes where intended. During testing, simulate controller input to validate every move—if Down sometimes skips an item, check navigation overrides and wrapping rules. Takeaway: explicit navigation beats implicit heuristics and improves accessibility for non-mouse players. In practical terms, ensure players can reliably move focus between widgets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Optimizing Complex UIs
screens.narratorSegment: Performance matters even in UIs. The most common mistake is relying on Event Tick inside UMG widgets to poll for state; instead favor event-driven updates so widgets react to changes only when necessary. Another important area is draw calls: each unique texture and material increases G P U work, so prefer texture atlases and shared materials for icons and button art. When toggling visibility often, prefer SetVisibility(Collapsed) to avoid repeated construction overhead. Break large widgets into child components so only affected parts update when state changes. Also be mindful of animations: lengthy or many overlapping animations can increase C P U and G P U load—limit concurrent animations and prefer simple opacity or transform changes rather than expensive material operations. A practical checklist: remove Tick where possible, profile UMG draw calls, consolidate small textures into atlases, and split heavy screens into smaller widgets. Misconception: micro-optimizing fonts or padding rarely helps; focus first on event-driven architecture and reducing unique materials. Takeaway: measure, then optimize—start by eliminating unnecessary per-frame updates and consolidating rendering resources. Optimizing Complex UIs means eliminate event tick in umg, consolidate textures, and use child widgets to limit updates to changed areas.. In practical terms, avoid event tick, reduce draw calls, and reduce texture variety. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 6 › Chapter 5.5 › UI Performance
Common Pitfalls
  • Using Event Tick to poll for changes instead of events or delegates.
  • Many unique textures and materials causing high draw calls.
  • Recreating widgets every toggle instead of reusing and collapsing.
Optimization Checklist
1. Replace Tick with delegates or event callbacks.
2. Profile UMG draw calls and merge small textures into atlases.
3. Split large UIs into child widgets and collapse unused parts.
4. Limit concurrent animations and prefer opacity/transform changes.
Key Takeaway

Start with event-driven updates and reduce unique rendering resources before micro-optimizing layout.

screens.title: Troubleshooting Input Conflicts and Sticky State
screens.narratorSegment: When UI and gameplay interact, bugs often look like sticky input, missing focus, or duplicated actions. Start debugging by logging your current input mode and cursor state at key points: when a menu opens, when it closes, and when a button is clicked. Check that SetInputMode is actually being called and that the widget pointer used in SetWidgetToFocus is valid. A frequent issue is calling SetInputMode before the widget is added to the viewport—when the engine cannot find the widget it may not set focus. Another problem is leaving bShowMouseCursor = true after resuming, which leaves the cursor visible and may change how mouse capture works. If clicks trigger both UI and in-world actions, verify whether GameAndUI is used and whether the UI consumes events. Use event handlers that return handled when appropriate. For controller navigation issues, ensure SetUserFocus is called on the owning player controller and that navigation rules are explicitly set for ambiguous layouts. Concrete steps: reproduce the bug, add logs for input mode and focus, step through TogglePauseMenu to validate order, and test with both keyboard and gamepad to confirm fixes. Takeaway: systematic logging and order-of-operations checks solve most input conflicts.

screens.title: Assessment: Inventory Interaction Scenario
screens.narratorSegment: For the assessment you'll design the input flow for an inventory screen that supports click-and-drag item management while preventing character movement. A common error students make is forgetting to hide the cursor on close or not returning focus to gameplay controls. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Here are the core concepts to carry forward. First, input modes determine where input is processed: GameOnly for gameplay, UIOnly for full UI control, and GameAndUI only when you intentionally need both. Second, focus and navigation must be explicit for predictable gamepad and keyboard behavior—use SetUserFocus, SetKeyboardFocus, and navigation rules. Third, bind widget animations to C++ with BindWidgetAnim and play them in NativeConstruct for consistent polish. Fourth, manage widget lifecycle for performance: prefer Collapsed for frequent toggles, RemoveFromParent to free memory for rare widgets, and avoid Event Tick in UMG. Finally, always test both keyboard and gamepad paths and log input mode and cursor state when troubleshooting. These rules reduce input conflicts, improve accessibility, and make UIs feel solid in play. Ask yourself: when I open a menu, should the player still move? Your answer determines the input mode and the user experience.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll build a practical mental model for input and UI lifecycle in Unreal Engine. You will learn the difference between directing input to the game, to the UI, or to both at once, and why that choice determines whether a player can still move, aim, or interact while a menu is open. We'll work toward a concrete implementation: a pause menu that pauses the game, shows the cursor, gains keyboard and gamepad focus, and plays a simple fade-in animation. Along the way I'll show you how to set explicit focus for predictable gamepad navigation and how to avoid common mistakes like leaving input modes in the wrong state or leaking widgets. We'll also discuss when to hide versus remove widgets, how to bind widget animations to C++ properties, and a short checklist for optimizing draw calls and avoiding Event Tick inside UMG. By the end of the lesson you'll understand the trade-offs behind input modes and have one ready-to-test pattern you can reuse for inventories, pop-ups, and overlays. Consider how your game should behave if the player presses a controller button while a dialog is open—that question will guide design.

By the end of this chapter you'll be able to configure input routing, manage widget focus for keyboard and gamepad, and design responsive UI patterns that avoid common pitfalls. First, you'll implement robust input handling by choosing between GameOnly, UIOnly, and GameAndUI and by toggling bShowMouseCursor so players have the right controls at the right time. Second, you'll manage UI navigation using SetUserFocus, SetKeyboardFocus, and explicit navigation rules so gamepad users never get stuck. Third, you will bind widget animations to C++ properties with BindWidgetAnim and trigger them from NativeConstruct to add polish. Finally, you'll learn performance strategies: prefer visibility states over destroying widgets when reused, avoid Event Tick inside UMG, and minimize draw calls with shared atlases. Each objective includes a concrete milestone: a working pause menu that pauses the game, shows the cursor, gains focus, and fades in cleanly. These competencies reduce input bugs, improve accessibility for non-mouse players, and keep your UI stable under stress. As you learn, compare your design decisions against player expectations: does opening a menu block movement? If not, reconsider the input mode.

This second objectives screen focuses on navigation and UI architecture you'll apply across menus and overlays. You will learn explicit focus management so that opening a menu reliably sets focus on the primary action for both keyboard and gamepad users. You'll practice SetUserFocus and SetKeyboardFocus to remove guesswork and set navigation rules inside UMG to avoid skipping elements. You'll also design and implement common UI patterns: pause menus that pause gameplay, inventory screens that lock input, overlay dialogs that temporarily capture focus, and loading screens that persist across level loads. For each pattern we'll discuss whether to use UIOnly or GameAndUI input and when to show the mouse cursor. Finally, you'll adopt performance habits: split complex screens into reusable child widgets, prefer Collapsed or Hidden visibility over removal when toggling frequently, and reduce unique textures to cut draw calls. A practical milestone is to wire up Resume and Quit buttons to call TogglePauseMenu and to test focus returning to the expected widget. These skills ensure accessible navigation and reliable behavior across controllers.

Input modes control whether input is handled by gameplay code, by widgets, or by both. GameOnly directs everything to the game, which is the default: movement, shooting, and camera controls remain active and UI widgets do not receive keyboard or gamepad input unless they explicitly request it. UIOnly sends all relevant input to the UI layer and disables gameplay input; this is ideal for full-screen menus and inventories where clicking, dragging, and keyboard navigation must be reliable. GameAndUI is a hybrid: it forwards input to both systems and can be useful for RTS-style interactions or context cursors. The important practical point is that GameAndUI often creates conflicts: a mouse click intended to press a UI button may also trigger a game action unless you consume the event. A common pattern is to switch to UIOnly and show the cursor when opening a menu, then restore GameOnly and hide the cursor when closing. Concrete example: when opening a pause menu you typically call SetInputMode(FInputModeUIOnly()) and set bShowMouseCursor to true; on resume, SetInputMode(FInputModeGameOnly()) and hide the cursor. Misconception to avoid: using GameAndUI to “be safe” usually leads to duplicate actions; prefer explicit consumption of input or UIOnly for modal dialogs. Takeaway: choose the strictest mode that matches your interaction model and manage cursor visibility and focus together.

Let's walk through the TogglePauseMenu implementation and the runtime consequences of each call. The pattern begins by checking a boolean bIsGamePaused. If paused, we resume gameplay: SetGamePaused(false), clear the pause widget from the viewport or hide it if you'll reuse it, set input back to GameOnly, and hide the mouse cursor. If not paused, we pause the game, create the pause widget via CreateWidget with a stored PauseMenuWidgetClass, AddToViewport, and then set the input mode to UIOnly. When using UIOnly you should call InputMode. SetWidgetToFocus with the widget's TakeWidget result so the engine knows where to send navigation events. Also set the mouse lock behavior as needed and set bShowMouseCursor to true. A concrete runtime example: press the Pause key, the game pauses, the menu fades in, the first button receives focus, and controller sticks move between buttons predictably. A common misconception is to RemoveFromParent() on every close; if you expect frequent toggles, prefer SetVisibility(Collapsed) so the widget remains in memory and costs less on reopen. Finally, ensure your resume path clears animation timers and any temporary input bindings to prevent stale state after unpausing. Try to test both keyboard and gamepad paths.

Widget animations provide important visual feedback and polish for menus and overlays. In UMG you author animations in the Designer and then bind them to C++ by adding a UPROPERTY marked Transient and meta=(BindWidgetAnim) of type UWidgetAnimation*. When the widget class is used as the blueprint parent, Unreal will populate that pointer if the animation name matches. In NativeConstruct you can detect the bound animation and call PlayAnimation to start it. A concrete example: create a FadeIn animation that adjusts Render Opacity from 0 to 1 over 0.5 seconds for your pause Canvas Panel. In the generated UMyPauseMenuWidget C++ subclass you add UPROPERTY(Transient, meta=(BindWidgetAnim)) UWidgetAnimation* FadeInAnimation; and in NativeConstruct call PlayAnimation(FadeInAnimation). A common misconception is that BindWidgetAnim magically creates animations; it only binds existing blueprint animations to the C++ pointer. Another pitfall is playing animations on a widget that hasn't been added to the viewport yet—ensure AddToViewport happens before relying on visible results, or play the animation inside NativeConstruct of the widget itself if it is constructed before AddToViewport. Takeaway: bind animations for predictable code-driven polish and always verify the animation pointer before calling PlayAnimation.

Choosing how to hide UI affects performance, memory, and state retention. RemoveFromParent completely removes the widget from the viewport and breaks its link to the widget tree: the object is typically eligible for garbage collection unless you keep a reference. This is good when you only show a widget once and want to free memory. Hidden keeps the widget in the hierarchy and reserves layout space, but it is not rendered; Collapsed keeps the widget in memory and removes it from layout so it consumes less render cost and no layout space. For frequently toggled UIs like a pause menu that opens many times per session, prefer Collapsed or Hidden because AddToViewport and construction are relatively expensive. A concrete example: if you RemoveFromParent every time and the player toggles the menu repeatedly, you will allocate and deallocate the widget repeatedly which can cause frame hitches. A common misconception is that Hidden equals zero cost; Hidden still keeps layout data and bindings active. Collapsed is often the best balance when you want the widget available but not visible. Takeaway: match the lifecycle to usage frequency—remove rarely used or large, persistent widgets and collapse frequently toggled ones to keep responsiveness.

Complex screens should be composed from smaller child widgets to improve maintainability and performance. Instead of a monolithic pause menu blueprint with dozens of elements and logic, split the UI into a header widget, a menu actions widget, and an optional settings pane. Each child can manage its own bindings, animation, and input handling. This modular approach reduces per-frame cost because only active child widgets update when necessary and you can reuse the same child across different parent screens. A concrete example: a reusable ButtonRow widget used in the pause menu and in the inventory context menus. When you change the visual style or behavior, you update it in one place and all parents benefit. Also, smaller widgets make navigation rules easier: set explicit navigation for each child so moving between rows is predictable. A common misconception is that more widgets always cost more—actually, smaller, reusable widgets can be cheaper than a large single widget because they localize bindings and reduce conditional logic. Takeaway: design with reuse in mind; child widgets are a both a code organization and a performance tool.

Performance matters even in UIs. The most common mistake is relying on Event Tick inside UMG widgets to poll for state; instead favor event-driven updates so widgets react to changes only when necessary. Another important area is draw calls: each unique texture and material increases G P U work, so prefer texture atlases and shared materials for icons and button art. When toggling visibility often, prefer SetVisibility(Collapsed) to avoid repeated construction overhead. Break large widgets into child components so only affected parts update when state changes. Also be mindful of animations: lengthy or many overlapping animations can increase C P U and G P U load—limit concurrent animations and prefer simple opacity or transform changes rather than expensive material operations. A practical checklist: remove Tick where possible, profile UMG draw calls, consolidate small textures into atlases, and split heavy screens into smaller widgets. Takeaway: measure, then optimize—start by eliminating unnecessary per-frame updates and consolidating rendering resources. When UI and gameplay interact, bugs often look like sticky input, missing focus, or duplicated actions. Start debugging by logging your current input mode and cursor state at key points: when a menu opens, when it closes, and when a button is clicked. A frequent issue is calling SetInputMode before the widget is added to the viewport—when the engine cannot find the widget it may not set focus. Another problem is leaving bShowMouseCursor = true after resuming, which leaves the cursor visible and may change how mouse capture works. Here are the core concepts to carry forward. First, input modes determine where input is processed: GameOnly for gameplay, UIOnly for full UI control, and GameAndUI only when you intentionally need both. Second, focus and navigation must be explicit for predictable gamepad and keyboard behavior—use SetUserFocus, SetKeyboardFocus, and navigation rules.
